en: Śrīḥ.
The Manual of Practice | First Chapter | May the Guru, who consists of consciousness and bliss, rise perpetually and perfectly within the space of my heart, dispelling the darkness of ignorance. (1)
Having bowed to Mārtāṇḍa and the other great masters, and by their grace, I shall write a certain manual for the calculation of the *guṇahāra*, *guṇa*, and so forth. (2)

He is skilled in manifold knowledge; he is as subtle as a sesame seed; he shines with the splendor of a great mountain; he is a noble lord of mountains with tusks like ivory; he possesses unsurpassed happiness; he is the most excellent one free from attachment; he is the lord of the fire-sticks of his staff-like arms; he has made the forest uneven [with his power]; he is weary from the waters of the crescent moon; he is the sun and other luminaries; he is the cycles of time; he is the earth and the days; he is compassionate; and he is the one who seeks the meaning of the digits of the moon for the sake of mortals. || 3 ||

The solar months are indeed the number of revolutions of the sun multiplied by six; the lunar months are simply the difference between the revolutions of the sun and the moon. The intercalary months of the yuga are the difference between the lunar and solar months; furthermore, these months multiplied by seven take on the form of days. (4)

The lunar months multiplied by seven and diminished by the terrestrial days (bhūdin) are the tithi-kṣayas (losses of lunar days). The solar revolutions increased by the terrestrial days are known as the sidereal days.

Thus, the revolutions of the spheres and so forth have been stated according to the Yuga-system for the purpose of calculating days within a Kalpa; for there are fourteen Manus here, and their Yugas are measured by the number Rāsa (six).
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—these are the names of the ages (yugas). In this Kalpa, the quarters of the ages (yugāṅghris) that have passed are measured by the number of Ādityas (twelve).
The Śaka years are obtained by adding the elapsed years, the current year, and the intercalary months, and then augmenting them with the time in days remaining in the current year. (8)

From the auspicious date (kalyandataḥ), subtracting the elapsed months and multiplying by the lunar month [count], one obtains the quotient of solar months. This is multiplied by eight (nāga) and added to the lunar tithis; then, divided by the lunar days multiplied by the number of earth-days (30), the result is the day-count (yugaṇa) starting from Sunday (acchavārāt).

The multiplicand, multiplied by the difference between the divisor and the multiplier, or else divided by the divisor, should be treated as positive or negative in the multiplicand according to whether the multiplier is greater or less [than the divisor], for the sake of obtaining the correct result. From the day-count (ahargaṇa), the planets in signs and so forth are obtained by dividing by the revolutions of the celestial bodies starting with earth; there, the Moon's apogee is increased by three signs, and Rāhu is subtracted from the circle (twelve signs). 11.

From the *Vāgbhaṭīya*, [the calculation is] from the Śaka year minus one hundred; from the degrees obtained by multiplying the minutes of arc by the slow velocity and subtracting the degrees, the bodies [of the planets] are diminished by the minutes of arc thus acquired. Chapter One. The [mean longitudes of the] planets starting with Mars, increased by the degrees obtained from the *māga* (multiplication) of the number of the calculator who has ascended to the knowledge of beauty, are to be combined with Mercury, Venus, and Saturn; Jupiter and Venus are excluded, as is the Sun. (12)

One should not divide by the divisor (hāra) beginning with Saturn; rather, having multiplied the [mean] longitude by the multipliers (guṇaka) stated here for the respective planets, one should divide by the divisors beginning with Saturn. The results obtained should be applied as minutes and so forth to the Moon and the other planets.

The quotient obtained from the number of elapsed Kali days by the divisor 136 is termed the *guṇya* (multiplier). That same number of elapsed Kali days, diminished by that [quotient], is termed the *khaṇḍa* (segment) for the planets. From the *guṇya* multiplied by its respective revolution-number, subtract the result divided by 27; these are the planets. Rāhu, however, is here [calculated] as the Sun plus three signs, minus six signs. (14)

From the [mean] planet multiplied by the number of lunar days (tithi) and further multiplied by the lord of the lunar days (tithīśa), one should subtract the portion obtained by multiplying by the mountain-doublers (72). Then, that [remainder], multiplied by the [current] multiplier (guṇa) starting with wealth (dhanādi), divided by the divisor starting with slow (mandādi), and reduced by the subtractive portion (hāra), should be applied as prescribed; thus those constants (dhruvas) shall exist in the minutes and so forth of the bird (the planet). || 15 ||

The divisor is obtained by dividing the number of days elapsed since the epoch by the number of lunar months; by that [divisor], the planets are calculated from their respective revolutions. In that [calculation], one should add three asterisms (three signs) to the Moon's apogee.
One should also apply half of that from the mandala; the group of five [digits] multiplied by the number of days in a lunar fortnight (bhūdi) is known as a khaṇḍa. || 17 ||

In that context, the [result] is respectively additive or subtractive, consisting of debt or wealth; this, when multiplied by its own respective mean anomaly and divided by the [mean] motion of the Sun, [yields the equation of center]. In the *Karaṇapaddhati*, [the correction] is multiplied by its own multiplier—whether positive and so forth—and divided by its own divisor for [the planets] beginning with Mars, according to the distinction between addition and subtraction.

Having sequentially converted wealth into debt and then reduced it by the divisor, one should apply the resulting degrees and so forth to the planets; then they shall become the terrestrial [longitudes] here. (20)

In the Śaka era reckoning, when the [true] apogee is subtracted from the [mean] apogee, it becomes the anomaly (tṛṇa); elsewhere than that, one should know it as the equation of the center (dhana) in its revolutions and so forth. 21.
The minutes of the zodiacal circle multiplied by the number of revolutions of the sun and other planets, divided by the terrestrial days, are known as their mean daily motions in minutes. || 22 ||

The daily motions of the Moon and other planets should be calculated as follows: from the solar longitude multiplied by its respective multiplier (such as wealth, etc. and divided by the number of days in a Mahāyuga, the results for each planet beginning with Saturn should be determined in successive order.

From the desired *kudina*, the divisor (*hāra*) is obtained by dividing by its own revolution-number (*paryaya*). The multiplier (*guṇa*) is that which, when multiplied by it, results in a value neither less nor greater than the [given] numerator; this is divided by the revolutions of the respective planet. In the case of Saturn (*saura*), having multiplied the divisor by the additive (or subtractive) constant and divided by the slow-motion divisor (*mandahāra*), one obtains the second divisor from the *kudina* days multiplied by this [result]. These multipliers, beginning with the additive, as determined by the Lord of Knowledge (*Jñānīndra*), are divided by the slow-motion divisors as previously stated; these operations must be performed upon the revolutions of the Moon and other planets, whereby they become the corrected revolutions. (Verse 25)

The sphere of the sky (ākāśakakṣyā) is the number of lunar mansions multiplied by the destroyer of ignorance (the number zero). From that, the daily distance traversed by the planets in *yojanas* is obtained by dividing by the days of the Creator (the number one). **Chapter Two** The orbit of the sky divided by its own revolution is the orbit of the great planets; the orbit of the sun multiplied by the number of policies (the number six) is declared by the wise to be the orbit of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Alternatively, the minutes of mean motion of the moon multiplied by two (the number two) are the daily distances in *yojanas* of the planets within their respective orbits. (27)

If this is the consumption of wealth (dhanabhukti), then the divisor for the planets is their own degree; if it is the motion in minutes (kalāgati), then the multiplier here is the divisor consisting of the minutes of the zodiacal circle (bhacakraliptā) in its own mean longitude.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Karaṇapaddhati.

Now begins the second chapter. The revolutions [of the planets], multiplied by their respective slow-motion divisors (mandādihāra) and increased or decreased by the products of the multipliers of Jñānendra, shall be multiplied by the factors such as *dhana* (additive). Furthermore, the days of the earth (civil days) divided by those same slow-motion divisors shall serve as the divisors; these aforementioned great multipliers and divisors are to be reduced by the common factor (*apavartya*). || 1 ||
When two quantities divide each other, the remainder shall be the *apavartana* (common divisor). The two quantities modified by that [divisor] are called the "firm" (*dṛḍha*) reduced quantities. (2)

From the great guṇa, the yugaṇa, and the desired [elapsed years], the planets beginning with the moon's [mean] longitude are derived; these, when combined with their respective constant values (*dhruvaka*) produced from the beginning of the Kali era, constitute the result; however, in that case, the number of the serpent (*phaṇi*, i.e., eight) must be subtracted from the constant. || 3 ||

From the [planetary] signs and so forth, from wealth and other qualities, and from the slow and other motions extracted, the Moon and other planets become [expressed as] minutes of arc and so on at the beginning of the Kali age in sequence. In the *Karaṇapaddhati*, among these, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Venus are to be subtracted again from the circle [of revolutions]; whereas for the Moon, the apogee is increased by three signs, and the node is increased by six signs. (4)

One should divide the two [quantities] that possess great qualities by each other; as long as there is a remainder upon division, one should place the resulting quotients and the remainders below one another in sequence. Having added the last [remainder] multiplied by the penultimate [quotient] to its own position above, one should discard that last [remainder]; this procedure should be repeated until the two quantities become the divisor and the quotient situated above.

One should place all the quotients and divisors obtained from mutual division one below the other in a single column. One should subtract the first quotient from the next, and likewise above them, perform the reduction of the sequence (avalī-upasaṃhṛti). This is done from the top, provided there is no prior annihilation; otherwise, that uppermost term should be discarded. Or, alternatively, by one's own choice, the remainders may be multiplied by the divisor. 6.

The two divisors are very small and possess great qualities; their difference is called *svarṇa* (gold). This is multiplied successively by the large divisor and divided by the small divisor when it is smaller, and by the large one when it is larger. That [result] is multiplied by the infinite city (*anantapura*) and divided by the product of the two divisors to obtain the second divisor. Likewise, from the remainder, the third divisor is obtained by dividing by the product of three divisors. || 7 ||

Alternatively, from the remainder arising from the mutual subtraction of the strings of the [two] longitudes, multiplied by the number of degrees in the great apogee (the Sun's apsis), and divided by that same [apogee], the resulting seconds—whether negative or positive—are known as the second [mean] longitudes. (8)

Those planetary revolutions (bhagaṇas) should be assumed as having large numerators, and likewise the terrestrial days (bhūdivasas) as having large denominators. In all cases, they should be made to have equal denominators at the time of their mutual conjunction or separation. Chapter Three. The multipliers and the divisors are multiplied by each other's divisors; thus the multiplier and the divisor become equal. There, one should multiply them by each other using the reduced divisors.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Karaṇapaddhati.

Now begins the third chapter. One should then combine the difference between the revolutions of the Moon and its apogee, as well as the series of [mean] motions starting from Earth; by means of these results, one should reduce them through the divisor of the multiplier, so that they become the [true] anomalies as previously described. (1)

From the moon’s apogee on the desired day—added to half the difference between the high points of the sun and the lord of the gods (the moon)—and having converted that into minutes of arc, one multiplies it by the square of the distance from the earth and divides by the square of the distance from the apogee; thus are the [corrections] obtained. (2)

Having multiplied by the "desired divisor" (abhīṣṭahāra) which has its upper part subtracted, and having divided by the previously mentioned "desired divisor," one should subtract from the lunar day-count (ghugaṇa) that which is greater or less therein, respectively, according to whether the divisor is even or odd. || 3 ||

The remainder is the fragment of the statement regarding the rising of the moon; the true moon for that day on the earth is thus [found], as are the fixed points (dhruvaka) of the planets, from which the true positions of the moon are calculated. || 4 ||

From the desired divisor, which is multiplied by the minutes of arc of the difference between the moon and its anomaly on that day, and divided by the center-divisor, the centers are obtained. When the moon is greater or less [than the anomaly], these are multiplied by the infinite series-sum and become positive or negative. The desired divisor and its multiplier mutually divide; the remainders of those multipliers and divisors are the divisors situated above the desired divisor, or else they are the positive and negative centers. (6)
This quality of the desired divisor has been stated; however, it must be divided when calculating the divisor for the refinement.
These centers would be the multipliers of the results held by their respective [planetary] lords, in due order. || 7 ||

Subtracting one's own ascendant from the Moon and adding all the [planetary] longitudes, one should divide by two, multiply by nine, and divide by eighty-one; the remainder from this division should be subtracted from the lunar day-count (yugana) to obtain the quotient of the segments as stated in the *Tuhinagovākya*. 8.

There, however, the obtained [value] multiplied by the time-serpent (kālanāga) should be divided by the glorious Saṅgaramya; the remainder, diminished by the subtractor (haran), becomes the group of days (dinagaṇa) or the segment of the statement (vākyakhaṇḍa). There, when the quotient is indeed struck by the gods (devara) and reduced by the fires of time (kālānala), one should discard the remainder from the count of days (dhugaṇa) for the sake of obtaining the segment stated in the statement regarding the snowy mountain (tuhinagiri).

The Third Chapter: From the difference between the moon and its apogee on that day, multiplied by the full heart-number (13) and divided by the minutes of the zodiacal circle, one obtains the value known as the *kendra*; for therein lies the true moon as a fixed point.

One should eliminate the remaining [coefficients] here by alternating their order, starting from the one declared by Śiva (the first) and the one that causes tremor (the last), which is difficult to conquer. For those [coefficients] surrounded by the auspicious, the true, the beautiful, and so forth, they become multipliers in the form of positive and negative values. (19)
One should clearly determine the Moon separately for each day, starting from one and increasing by one up to the number of the lords of the gods (thirty-three), in order to establish that statement.

When the Moon's ascensional difference (nīcakaṇḍa) has been subtracted from its altitude as prescribed, it is the sum of the Moon's altitude and its ascensional difference; due to the excess over the desired divisor (iṣṭahāra), that sum approaches the time of sunrise. || 13 ||

The *ghaṭī*-seconds arising from the interval between [the previous] conjunction and sunrise are multiplied by the sine of the desired argument divided by the divisor increased by the sine of its maximum amplitude for that day, and then divided by the radius; these are the *ghaṭī*-seconds produced by the interval between conjunctions and sunrise, being positive or negative according as the Moon is greater or less [than the Sun]. (14)

When refined by those [corrections] for the breaths practiced with their own qualities and obtained through their own subtraction, these two moons shall become equal to what are called the fixed points of conjunction (yogadhruva).

In the same manner, one should again bring together the sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon at the desired time, using the formula: "by means of the days of terrestrial time equal to the interval between the mean positions of the planets at the desired time and the intervals between the revolutions of the desired planet," as stated in the *Phalaṇapaddhati*. This is the third chapter. 16.

In the Karaṇapakṣatī, now begins the fourth chapter. The divisors for finding the mean [longitude] of birds other than the Moon should be known as those of the slow anomaly; for Mercury and Venus, they are the same as those of the Sun.

One should divide the difference between the revolutions of the Sun and the desired planet by the terrestrial days; the divisors here should be multiplied by their respective results, and these become the divisors for the moving apogees. (2)

From the mean longitude of the planets, subtracted by their own apogee and by their perigee, and from the mean longitude subtracted by the apogee, one should derive the equation-parts using the respective "subtractors of the anomaly" (kendra-haras) as described for the Moon; thus they are determined according to the rules of calculation.

In the case of a statement regarding a subtraction of factors, the divisor is always greater; when the factor exceeds the divisor, one should proceed with the results [obtained] by subtracting the divisor and so forth. (4)

The divisor (*hāra*) is the difference between the revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) of the Sun and Venus; it is a small multiplier. From those two, the divisors here are produced by their mutual product, multiplied by the Earth-divisor (*dharāhā*). Divided by that divisor, as stated in the rule for the operation of the sentence, they become the revolutions (*maṇḍala*). Likewise, from the repeated multiplication of the remainders of the cycles (*cakrakalikā*) obtained through mutual division, the constant values (*dhruva*) are determined as positive or negative.

The necklace-bearers are those who have been brought into the calculation of the mandala; by means of them, one should cause [the result] to be purified, or else by means of small mandalas together with the constant [additive].

The number of desired days, diminished by the quotient obtained from the difference between the [mean] motion and the swifter apogee, shall be the time of the conjunction of the swifter apogee and the planet. (7)

The difference between the [mean] revolutions and the product of the desired days multiplied by the minutes of arc of the non-oscillating (fixed) apogee, divided by the number of civil days, is subtracted from the unknown revolution-count; the remainder is the time of the conjunction of the mean planet and the movable apogee. || 8 ||

The bird (planet) situated in the middle of that period, diminished by its own soft [sign] and exaltation, is converted into minutes; it is multiplied by the desired [number] and divided by the divisor of its own mandala, then multiplied by the infinite city (100,000) and divided by the product of the desired upper and lower divisors. || 9 ||

Chapter Four. The difference between the fewer and the greater [days] here, divided by the interval between the revolutions of both, is to be subtracted from the time of the conjunction of the mean planet and the swifter apogee; thus it becomes the day to be subtracted for the planets. (10)

The difference between the mean planet at that time and its slowest velocity is the *śodhyadhruva*, designated as positive or negative depending on whether the mean planet is greater or less than the apogee. (11)

When the mean planet and the apogee are similar [in their motion], one should take the difference in minutes between them; this should be divided by the mean planet when it is less than the apogee, or by the apogee when it is greater. The remainder is the "days of subtraction" (*śodhyadina*). These are multiplied by the constant result (*dhruvaphala*) and subtracted from the corresponding orbital circle (*tanmaṇḍala*) at the time when the mean planet and the apogee become equal, for the sake of obtaining the respective subtrahends.

In the *Karaṇapaddhati*, the time for the conjunction of the mean planet and the swift apogee is combined with half the number of days stated for the period of retrogression (*mauḍhya*). The day-count (*yugaṇa*) at the end of retrogression is accompanied by its fractional part; furthermore, in the case of retrogression, the divisors are the divisors of the moving anomaly (*calakendra*). (13)

The divisor and the multiplier are the revolutions of the planet and the sun, respectively; one should divide those two by each other. The divisors resulting from that [division] become those stated in the mathematical treatises. (14)
Having subtracted the small motion from the great motion of the midheaven and the sun brought together at the end of midday, the remainder is converted into *kalās*. (15)

When the stated divisors have been disregarded, the result is multiplied by the desired [number] and divided by the minutes of arc of the circle; this is then again multiplied by the divisor for the desired [time] above.

Having subtracted that [result] from the desired divisor—whether it be less or more—one should discard [the remainder] from the Śaka year according to the requirement of being joined with twice the desired divisor. (17)

At the end of the remaining years, there occurs a conjunction between the desired planet and the sun; therefore, that year which is subtracted as stated in the calculation is called the "subtracted year" (śobhyābda). || 18 ||

The intercalary months from the beginning of the Kalya era, multiplied by the revolutions of the sun and divided by terrestrial days, are subtracted from the fixed lunar constant at the start of the Kalya era multiplied by terrestrial days; the remainder is divided by those intercalary months. The result is the number of days. This is the segment for the intercalary months as stated; then, the divisors are formed by the product of the intercalary months and terrestrial days, and these serve as the divisors therein. (19)

Fifth Chapter: Then, having multiplied the number of lunar months in a yuga by two, and having added the sum of the revolutions of the sun and the node, one should derive the divisor from the results obtained here. These [results], when multiplied by the number of terrestrial days and divided by the lunar months, become the divisors mentioned for eclipses. (20)

Having added the midday sun and moon and the [longitude of the] serpent [Rāhu] at the end of the middle node-period, multiply the degrees traversed by the sun and moon by nine and divide by the minutes of the zodiac; multiply that by the position of the eclipse and divide by nine—the remainder, multiplied by terrestrial days and divided by lunar months, gives a result which, when subtracted from the total number of days, yields the segments as stated for the eclipse.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Karaṇapaddhati*.

Now begins the fifth chapter. Those planets which have been well-examined through eclipses and planetary conjunctions—whether their revolutions and other parameters are equal to those observed or are to be calculated for a Kalpa—are considered equal to what is seen. || 1 ||
The difference between the observed planet and that brought forth by the astronomical system should be converted into minutes and multiplied by the solar revolutions as stated for the Kalpa. (2)
The years situated between the time of the *tantra-nirmāṇa* and the time of the *parīkṣā-samaya* are multiplied by the results of the zodiacal wheel. (3)

Having subtracted the [mean] longitude of the planet derived from the tantra from the elapsed years of the kalpa multiplied by its revolutions and divided by the solar revolutions of the kalpa, one obtains the mean [longitude] starting from the zodiacal signs (bhagaṇa). Having discarded that, they call the remainder—the residue remaining after subtracting the bird (the sun) at the end of the examined year—the so-called "fixed point at the beginning of the kalpa" (kalpamukhadhruva). || 5 ||

From the product of the years elapsed since the beginning of the Kalpa by the days of the Earth (bhūdivasa) as stated for the Kalpa, divided by the solar revolutions (bhagaṇa) as stated for the Kalpa, the remainder obtained after dividing by seven—when subtracted from the end of the Prabhava year—is this constant of transit (saṃkramaṇadhruva) arising at the start of the Kalpa.

The differences [of the sun] brought forth by the tantras and examined are multiplied by the separate days of the kalpa and by the revolutions of the planets as stated in the Kalpa; these are then reduced to breaths (prāṇas) by the years of the solar kalpa. These breaths are the *kalikās* in the planets of transits, starting from the beginning of the kalpa. If the examined sun is slightly less or greater than that, they become the true [values]. (7)

In this way, however, the permanent existence [of the self] at the beginning of a kalpa is not at all tenable; therefore, another conditioning factor (saṃskāra) is postulated as the means to avoid that [fault]. (8)

Having subtracted from one another the multitude of years elapsed since the beginning of the Kalpa and the solar revolutions occurring within that Kalpa, and having multiplied the fixed celestial degrees (dhruvāṃśas) at the start of the Kalpa by the desired number of years obtained through division, [one arrives at the result]. || 9 ||

Fifth Chapter. Having multiplied the previously stated [value] by the desired divisor, and having multiplied it again by the upper divisor, the remainder—whether positive or negative—is determined according to whether the pair of divisors is even or odd. || 10 ||

When the multitude of synonyms for the "refined" (saṃskṛta) has arisen according to the [astrological] era, one should perform that [calculation] so that the planet shall be its true (sphuṭa) value. The planet, multiplied by the desired [factor], diminished or increased by the divisor, and joined with the aspect, is sometimes equal to the aspect itself; for it is thus that the planet may become identical to the aspect. || 11 ||

The apogee of that [planet] is likewise reduced by those two divisors and increased by the divisor of the apsis; this should be subtracted from the divisor if it is negative, for in the case of the apsis, everything is indeed reversed. (12)

The number of years elapsed since the beginning of the kalpa, as well as the number of solar revolutions in seven days, should be multiplied by each other; then, having subtracted [the result] from there, the *ikās* (intercalary days) are to be calculated.

In those *hāra*s, one should again multiply by the desired [number] from the day of the transition at the beginning of the kalpa; then divide by seven. That result, multiplied by the desired upper *hāra* and reduced by the divisor, should be applied as positive or negative to the kalpa-day as previously described. || 14 ||
The wise postulate the measurement of the kalpas and so forth in many ways; for it is because the restriction applies only to the goal (upeya) and not to the means (upāya). (15)

In the Kalpa of the Karaṇapaddhati, some maintain that there are one thousand Yugas; therein, seventy-one Yugas belong specifically to the Manus. Furthermore, at the beginning and end of each Manvantara, as well as in the intervals between them, there are Sandhyās (twilight periods) equal to four-tenths of a Yuga.

There were fourteen Manus in the Kalpa, and their Yugas were equal in duration to that of Pṛthu. Three Yugas have passed since the beginning of creation; others say that there will likewise be [three] after the dissolution.
The tenth part of the Yuga, multiplied by the number of enjoyments (bhoga-priya) in sequence, shall be the measure of the Kṛta and the other ages within these two fortnights. 18.
In this kalpa, during the twenty-eighth cycle of the Vaivasvata Manu, it is traditionally held that the Kali age prevails here in its entirety.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Karaṇapaddhati.

Now begins the sixth chapter. From Vyāsa divided by four, multiplied many times separately by three, five, seven, and so on, and divided by the respective yugas; when added to or subtracted from Vyāsa divided by four in due order, one shall obtain the very subtle circumference.

From the diameter multiplied by the square root of five, subtracting the square roots of four, two, and one respectively, and then adding or subtracting these values from the diameter multiplied by three in successive order, the circumference should be calculated.
The Sixth Chapter || 3 ||

One should remove the difference between the squares by subtracting the smaller from the larger, or one may remove it by subtraction through the square root. To obtain the sum or difference of the results derived from two pairs of squares, one should divide the product of the diameter and six by the sum of the squares increased by twice the number of terms minus one, or by the even-numbered squares subtracted from the squared values. When the diameter multiplied by three is divided by that result, the circumference shall then be obtained.
From this great desired *vyāsa*, the squares of the two sides divided by each other should be multiplied by the factors as stated; those are then the *vyāsa*-squares. (5)

By means of those [factors] which have become the divisor of the qualities and which have been subtracted as stated, one should bring the subtraction from the desired arc; from the subtraction, the addition is obtained by reversal.

The minutes of arc (kalās) of the apsis, multiplied by one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, and twelve, and divided respectively by twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six, forty-eight, sixty, seventy-two, eighty-four, ninety-six, one hundred and eight, one hundred and twenty, and one hundred and thirty-two, will yield the [mean] anomaly, its half, and the sine of the anomaly. (7)
The sine of one sign is half the radius; the square root of half the square of the radius is the sine of one and a half signs. From these two, one should derive the other sines.

The square root derived from the sum and difference of the squares of the trijyā (radius) and the jyā (sine) of three times the greatest [arc] are, respectively, the sines of the desired half-chord and its complement. (9)

In the Karaṇapaddhati, it is taught that half of the square root of the sum of the squares of the versed sine (iṣṭa) and the chord (cāpa-guṇa) is the multiplier for the desired semi-chord (iṣṭa-dhanur-ardha-guṇa). The side (koṭi) is the square root of the difference between the squares of the respective [semi-chord] and its triple; the two sides [the semi-chord and its triple] added to or subtracted from that [side] are the respective arrows (vāṇa).

When the square of half the diameter is increased by or decreased by half the product of the desired arrow and the versed sine, and that result is halved, it becomes the product of the sine and the cosine of half the desired arc. (11)

And from the arc, as well as from its respective result, it is likewise; from the square root of three multiplied by the arc diminished by the arc, the resulting pairs of values are placed one below the other, starting from the arc and extending to half the diameter. (12)

Having placed [the values] one above the other, one should discard them; the remainders shall be the products of the arms and the hypotenuse. From the fractions obtained by multiplying the number starting from one with the divisor, there will thus be twenty-four sines. (13)

The wise one, possessing the strength of a young elephant, a multitude of monkey-lords, devoted to all goals, steady, and free from fear, [should proceed] with these five [parameters] bound by the king’s fetters in sequence. Having multiplied the lowest [value] by the desired bow-length and divided by the last [value], the quotient should be subtracted from the top [value]; then, by means of this wealth, [the process continues] until finally reaching the bow-length.

The Sixth Chapter. [The sequence of] *stena*, *strīpiśuna*, *sugandhinaga*, *nudbhadra*, *aṅgabhavyāsana*, *manāṅga*, *narasiṃha*, *ūnadhanakṛt*, and *bhū* [is used] for the feet and syllables (*pada*). From the desired bow-length multiplied by the lower [value], having performed the operation of division by the last [value], the quotient is to be subtracted from the upper [value]; thus the result will be the last [term] of the sequence. (15)

The sine of the third [arc] is the radius (trijyā) divided by the difference between the last and the penultimate sines; this becomes the divisor here. The first sine, diminished by its own fractional part and doubled, becomes the second sine. That same sine, doubled and diminished by the first sine divided by its own divisor, becomes the third sine; in this manner, the subsequent ones, beginning with the fourth, should be calculated.

The square of the difference between the first desired sine and the arc is divided by the desired sine and the arc; the resulting quotient is the arc above the desired sine, and from this, the first desired sine and arc itself is obtained. || 17 ||

From the product of the desired multiplier and half the radius, divide by ten million to obtain the first result; multiply that first result by the square of the sine and obtain the respective subsequent results. Having squared the multiplier of ten million, divide those results by one, three, five, and so on, respectively; add them together for odd places and subtract for even places. The resulting sum shall be the sine and the arc. || 18 ||

The square root of half the square of the width, diminished by the portion of the base corresponding to its own arc, is the remaining arc; from that, the chord is obtained, and the square of half the chord is the negative bow (asaddhanuḥ). || 19 ||

In the *Karaṇapaddhati*, the upajāti [sine] is the cube root of one, two, three, and so on, up to the number of desired sines, multiplied by the square of the radius; it is then diminished by the seconds of arc corresponding to the day-count. (20)

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Karaṇapaddhati*. Now begins the seventh chapter: The singing of the Sun, the position of the Moon, the minutes of arc of the true epicycle at all times, Vandyo, Divyo, Guṇī, Kṛṣṇa, Sūnu, Mānī, and Kalādhara. (1)

Position, charity, austerity, honor, the sun, the wise, the base, and the equal; the wealthy, the world, wealth, charity, Mars, and the paridhi-likās—these are the values for the odd and even quadrants (kendras) according to the sequence of slow and fast [planets]. They are stated individually for each quarter (pāda), having been reduced by the Asuras. (3)

Having multiplied the sine of the arm by the interval between the arcs, and having divided [the result] by three sines in the circle of mean velocity, one obtains the fruit respectively as positive or negative in the circle of true velocity, depending on whether the true velocity is less or greater [than the mean], for the sake of establishing the true circle. (4)

The slow-motion (mānda) correction for the sun and other planets is obtained by multiplying the desired sine (dorguṇa) by the slow-motion equation of the center (sphuṭavṛtta) and dividing by nine; this result is then added to the [mean] sine. || 5 ||

The remaining [sine] of the arm (bhuja) multiplied by the true circumference and divided by nine yields two results; those are the diameter and the sine of the arm. That [diameter] is the arc here, being positive in Capricorn and so on, and negative in Cancer and so on. Having added the square of that arc to the square of the result of the arm, the square root thereof is the swift hypotenuse (śīghrakarṇa). From the result of the arm multiplied by the trijyā and divided by that [hypotenuse], the resulting arc is the sine of the arm in Cancer, Capricorn, and so forth.

The products of the desired sine of the co-latitude multiplied by the circumference of the apsis and divided by nine should be the results for the sine of the co-latitude; or one should perform the correction of the circle for these two.

From two [sines], they say one should then take the sine of the arc and its corresponding cosine; first, however, the sine of the complement (koṭijyā) is multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the arc, and the result is the arrow (bāṇa). From half the arrow and also from half the sine of the arc, one takes the product of the circumference and the divisor (the number of divisions), divides by nine, and adds it to the sine of the arc and the sine of the complement respectively. When these are equal or greater, they become the corrected [sines]. (8)

In the case of Mars, the arc resulting from the arm [sine] thus brought forward is clearly applied; in the case of the hypotenuse, it is multiplied by the radius (trijyā), divided by the hypotenuse, and likewise converted into an arc. || 9 ||
For those whose conduct is clear and who have struck down the fire of desire, there shall be the attainment of the final fruit through the power of their touch.

Subtracting or adding the result of the cosine-sine (koṭijyā) [to or from the radius] according to the application of the sign starting from Cancer, one should multiply by Kaṇāṇḍamuni as stated in the *Mūla*. In the *Karaṇapaddhati*, the sine (dorjyā) is likewise corrected by the cosine (koṭikā) increased by the radius; its arc, subtracted from the arcs of the sine and cosine, is the sine starting from Cancer. If the cosine-sine is less than the final result in Cancer and so on, it should be multiplied by the radius and divided by the arc of the sine multiplied by the hypotenuse (karṇa).
Let the arc of the corrected cotangent, increased by two signs, be subtracted from half the circle; likewise, let the arc of the square of the sine be subtracted from the arc of the cotangent. (12)
Alternatively, the sine of the argument multiplied by the hypotenuse and converted into an arc shall here be the maurvikā for Cancer, Leo, and the subsequent signs. (13)

The last term multiplied by ten million and divided by two, when multiplied by that same last term and added to the square of half the circumference, becomes the hypotenuse here when its square root is extracted. (14)

From the result of the [longitude] of Capricorn, Cancer, and so forth, one subtracts the arc of that arm (bhuja) and adds it; the resulting multiplier of the arm is used to divide the sine of the result of the arm multiplied by the radius. The quotient here is the [correction for] the swift epicycle. (15)

The arc derived from the sine of the final side shall be the final arc when the odd position is reached; the arc derived from the sine of the first side, doubled and diminished by the final [arc], shall be the first [arc]. (16)

Having subtracted the apogee of the slow planet from the true longitude of the end of the sign, one should take the sine (doḥ) and cosine (koṭi) values. Then, multiplying those two by three respectively and dividing by nine, the results shall be the sine and cosine corrections (phala). [Chapter Seven]

The square root of ten million multiplied by the sine of the arc produced from [the longitude of] Capricorn, Sagittarius, and so forth, having been made positive or negative according to the odd or even nature of the trine (trimaurvikā), and added to the square of that [sine], is the hypotenuse (karṇa) here when the order is reversed. (18)

The result obtained by dividing the sine-fruit (doḥphala) multiplied by the trijyā by this [radius] is converted into arc; starting from Aries or Libra, one should apply it as positive or negative respectively when the sun is in the latter half of the sign. Then, the mean sun at the moment of the transit (saṅkramaṇa) will be obtained. || 19 ||

In this very same manner, one should derive the mean [longitude] of the Sun and Moon from their desired true [longitudes]. Therein, the square of the radius (trijyā) divided by the aforementioned inverse hypotenuse (vyastakarṇa) is the slow hypotenuse (mṛduśruti). || 20 ||
The radius of the sun's orbit, known as the clear yojana-ear, is derived from the circumference of the orbit divided by its revolution and multiplied by the fraction of the circle. (21)

Thereafter, from the midpoint of the sun's transit calculated by the division [of the year], increased by the result of the arm [of the sun] at the end of the year and multiplied by terrestrial days, the statement for the month is indeed obtained by dividing with solar days; here, the remainder is the statement for the transit (saṅkrānti), which is its friend.

In this very same manner, from the mean sun calculated as the precise end of a lunar mansion, one should apply the statement regarding the transit into a lunar mansion as previously stated by the sages.

From the beginning of the month, the eight-day intervals arising from the difference in degrees between the true and mean suns—these eight-day intervals are suitable for the "Karaṇapaddhati" and other such works; their duration in days is determined by whether they are additive or subtractive, depending on the increase or decrease in the number of days. (24)

From the apsis of Mars and the other planets, the equation of anomaly is derived from the anomaly-sector; this is added to or subtracted from the mean [longitude] reckoned from its apogee to obtain the true slow motion. For Venus and Mercury, one should apply their own slow equation to their respective mean longitudes—calculated from the difference between the mean longitude and the maximum [longitude]—multiplied by nine and divided by the true fast epicycle; that result shall be the true slow motion.

Having calculated the sines of the [true] arguments by subtracting their respective moving degrees from the [true] anomalies minus two signs, one should divide those [sines] multiplied by the radius by the apogee-sine; then the true [mean] anomaly will be obtained. One should also calculate the [true] apsis by subtracting the apogee from the mean and the true [mean] anomalies; where the true [mean] anomaly is obtained through the tabulated equation-of-center, there the calculation of the [true] anomaly is likewise performed through the calculation of the [true] apsis.

But when the anomaly is in the first or last quadrant—that is, in Capricorn, Cancer, and so forth—the manda-karṇa (manda-equation radius) is derived from the anomaly multiplied by three and divided by nine, increased by the sine of that anomaly. When it is in the second or third quadrant, the śīghra-karṇa (epicycle radius) for Mars and the other planets is obtained by multiplying the difference between the anomaly and six signs by the radius and dividing by the sine of the anomaly; for the Moon, the śīghra-karṇa is always the final karṇa.

The difference between the planet and the center, multiplied by three and divided by the two ears (karṇas), is the ear (karṇa) of the deficient [arc]; this is the seventh chapter. One should know that the distance from the center of the earth to the planet is indeed that same value; for the moon, it would generally be precisely that. || 28 ||

One's own circumference, multiplied by the distance between the Earth and the planet and divided by the radius of the epicycle of the swifter [planet], becomes the *yojana*-karṇa for Mercury and Venus; and for the others, it is that same value divided by the number of degrees [in their respective epicycles]. (29)

From Mars, the results [of the anomaly] arising from the ignorance [of the equation] are increased ten-million-fold and multiplied by its own swift epicycle; when divided by nine, these are the results. The square root of the difference between the squares of the sine and the result, added to the cosine result, shall be the radius (karṇa) for the slow-moving planets, the gods, and the serpents, in the vicinity of their rising and setting times. (30)

The product of the sine and cosine of the portion arising from the [mean] anomaly, diminished by the [mean] Mercury and Venus respectively, multiplied by the sine of the [true] anomaly and divided according to the difference in the eccentric circles—having subtracted that same final correction derived from the fast epicycle divided by the velocity circle—the remainder shall be the true final correction. || 31 ||

From that [square], subtracting the square of the hypotenuse (dōrguṇa), take the square root; then add or subtract it from the square of the side (koṭiguṇa). Thus, generally, the hypotenuse for the signs beginning with Capricorn and Cancer, ending with Pisces and Virgo respectively, will be obtained. (32)
This *karṇa* shall be the divisor of the difference at the beginning and end of the *moṭhī*; for it is indeed the maximum *kṣepa*, or else those two [values] reduced by a common factor.
Āsura, Nāla, Āraṇya, Anta, and Āśraya, which are unpleasant; these are, respectively, the maximum subtractive *liptās* for the Moon and the other [planets]. (34)

In the *Karaṇapaddhati*, the diameter of the sun's disc shall be in yojanas; likewise, that of the moon and the earth shall be one-fourth [of the sun's]. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Karaṇapaddhati*. Now begins the eighth chapter: The palashrutis (degrees of ascensional difference) are stated as being increased by the bhava when they fall at the midpoint of the equinoctial day. [This is] from the product of the midpoint of the equinoctial day... 35.
The chord corresponding to that [arc] is derived from the three qualities divided by that [same quantity].

The square root of the difference between the squares of those two [sines] is the sine of the parallax (lambana-maurvikā). Some desire this correction for the sake of making those two mutually precise. (2)

The product of the equinoctial shadow multiplied by half the terrestrial diameter, divided by the trijyā (radius), is subtracted from half the diameter of the sun's orbit; the remaining result is multiplied by the latitude and co-latitude [sines] respectively. One should then divide these by the current semi-diameter of the sun's orbit; the results obtained are the [corrected] latitude and co-latitude multipliers, which are positive or negative according to the sequence. Thus, they become precise. || 3 ||

There, the shadow of the sun, measured in finger-breadths according to one's desired scale, should be applied to the light of the great gnomon (mahāśaṅku) after it has been corrected, just as in the case of the observer at the equator (lambakākṣa).
The hypotenuse and the base, multiplied by the shadow-fingers, become the clear *mahābhaya*; when multiplied by the shadow-fingers, they become the *mahābhava* and the *āhukoṭika*. (5)
The shadow's east-west component is the *koṭi*, while its north-south component is the *bhuja*. When the sun is on the equatorial plane, there is neither *bhuja* nor *koṭi* at midday.

Chapter Eight. When the sun is on the equinoctial point, the sine of latitude (akṣajīvā) is obtained by multiplying the sine of declination (apakrama) by the radius (trijyā) and dividing by the shadow (śaṅku). Alternatively, the difference between the arcs of the midday shadow and the declination is the arc of latitude; however, in the intermediate directions, their sum is the arc of latitude.

When two arcs, having desired multipliers, are multiplied by each other’s versine, their sum and difference shall be equal to the product of the sum and difference of the arcs of the desired multipliers, respectively. (8)

The square of the sum of the shadow and the base, increased by the square of the difference of their products, is divided by the product of the hypotenuse and the base; from this, the greater or lesser of these two [quantities] multiplied by the trijyā (radius) becomes the *lambajyā* (sine of colatitude), and its complement is the *koṭi*. (9)

The quotient obtained from the square of the semi-diameter divided by the true lambajīvā (sine of the colatitude) is declared to be the divisor for one's own location; that is called the inverse colatitude (vyastalamba). || 10 ||

The correction (guṇa) is produced from twenty-four parts; the sine of the desired [longitude] is multiplied by that maximum declination (parāpama) and divided by the radius (trijyā). The resulting multiplier of the declination (kāntiguṇa) shall be the vikā of the day-maker (the Sun), derived from its cosine. || 11 ||

One should divide the product of the arm by the sine of the desired arc; the quotient, converted into an arc and subtracted from the arc of the arm, shall be the interval in breaths and minutes. || 12 ||

The square root of the difference between the square of the arm and nine times the square of the earth, multiplied by the maximum oblique distance (parāpakrama) and divided by the sine of latitude (yujyā), as found in the Karaṇapaddhati, is the interval of breath-units (prāṇakalā); this is positive or negative according to the sequence of even and odd quarters.

Having multiplied the square root of the versed sine by ten million, one should divide it by the desired arc-sine; the result obtained, when converted into an arc, or alternatively, when subtracted from the arc of ten million, shall be the difference in *prāṇakalās*. (14)
The apamā [latitude] is multiplied by palavyayā and divided by svalambaka; then, the result is multiplied by trijīvā and divided by ghujīvā to obtain the carārdha [ascensional difference]. (15)

The sine of time (kālajīvā) divided by the product of the desired day-count (iṣṭayugaṇa) and the cosine of the desired ascensional difference (iṣṭadorjyā), multiplied by the ascensional difference (cara), or else that same value multiplied by the ascensional difference and divided by the sine of three signs (tribhajīvā), is the sine of the ascensional difference (carajyā). || 16 ||

Having multiplied the product of the trijyā and the latitude by the divisor obtained from the avakṣepaka, one should divide the product of the sine of the oblique ascension and the sine of the amplitude by the celestial hypotenuse (yumauryā). The quotient obtained shall be the carajyā (sine of the carakhaṇḍa); the arc of that [sine] shall indeed be the carāsus (carakhaṇḍas in time units). || 17 ||

The product of the radius of the celestial sphere and the sine of latitude, divided by the product of the desired sine of the amplitude and its corresponding cosine, shall be the carajyā; that is Māyā, derived from the arc of the inclination. (18)

The final amplitude (antyāpama) is obtained by dividing the final additive (antyakṣepa) multiplied by the sine of the final argument (antyadhujyā) by the radius (trijyā). Then, the sine of the complement (koṭijyā), multiplied by the final additive and divided by the radius, [is used]. (19)

One should multiply by the sine of the argument (pharka) and divide by the radius (krānti) to obtain the final result; when that is multiplied by the sine of the arm (bāhu) and the sine of the complement (koṭi), and divided by the radius (trijyā), the results are the sines of the arm and the complement respectively.

The eighth chapter: The golden [triangle] arising from the koti is formed in succession starting from the hypotenuse (mṛga) and the base (kari). The square root of the sum of the squares of its two arms is the hypotenuse (karṇa) here, produced from Rāhu.
The result of the arm, multiplied by the trijyā, should be divided by the radius of Rāhu; the arc of the quotient shall be known as the moon's *vikṣepacalana*.
One should divide the maximum oblique ascension (paramāpakrama) multiplied by the sine of the latitude (rāhukaṇa) by the trijīvā; the result shall be the maximum amplitude (paramakrānti) of the moon.

The sine of latitude (yujyā) multiplied by the square of the trijyā and divided by the equinoctial shadow (akṣakarṇa), then diminished by the quotient obtained by dividing that same product by the trijyā—these resulting sines of the ascensional differences (mānya) and so forth, when reduced to the local latitude, become the divisor-sines (hārajīvā) for the sun. (24)

The dust-colored [shadow] on the earth is the result of the sun's orb being struck by a portion of its circle; from the daily travel in yojanas, the divisor for the depression (lamvana) is obtained. || 25 ||

The correction (lambana) in nāḍīs and so forth is obtained by dividing the trijyā by the lambha-hara; that same value, diminished by the degrees of motion, is to be subtracted from the observer's height (nara) in the calculation of shadow.

The difference between the minutes of arc of the motions of the Sun and the Moon, diminished by the minutes of arc of the zodiacal circle, reduced by the Earth’s semi-diameter, and divided by the minutes of arc of the Moon’s motion multiplied by sixteen; this, multiplied by the half-sum of the sine of the latitude and the sine of the maximum declination, and divided by the radius, yields a result which, when multiplied by the local latitude and divided again by the radius, is called the correction for parallax arising from the *carāvalambana*. || 27 ||

In the *Karaṇapaddhati*, one should subtract the square of the latitude (*cara*) from the square of the radius (*trijyā*), add the square of the "resultant fruit" (*caramaphala*), and take twice the cosine-sine (*koṭijyā*) with its body increased by the "resultant fruit. The square root of that is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). One should divide the sine of the argument multiplied by the radius by this hypotenuse; the result obtained are the multipliers for the parallax as recited in the treatise on eclipses. (28)

The sine of the latitude (bhujaguṇa) multiplied by ten million and divided by this [result], or else the sine of the latitude multiplied by the radius of the celestial sphere (trijyā) and divided by that same [result], yields the degrees of the depression (lambana) as declared by the beloved woman. This [depression] is devoid of the variegated beauty of breasts struck by the hand, and it is like the garland of the Malaya mountain used in amorous play. || 29 ||

From the square root obtained by subtracting the product of the sine of the amplitude and the sine of the ascensional difference from the product of the radius and the sine of the amplitude—divided by that same product of the sine of the amplitude and the sine of the ascensional difference—and multiplied by the sine of the latitude, one obtains the sines of the oblique ascensions, beginning with the time of sunrise, for a yogī who is fearful of the speech consisting mostly of wisdom and delusion. (30)
The *yojanas* of Viṣkambha and the others, when multiplied by the [mean] velocity and divided by the clear *yojana*-radius (*sphuṭayojanakarṇa*), are known as their *kalās*. (31)
Alternatively, the degrees of true motion multiplied by the yojanas of the diameter of the orb, and divided by the daily motion in yojanas, become the minutes [of arc] for the Sun and the Moon. (32)

The degrees of the Moon's motion multiplied by sixty thousand yojanas, diminished by the Sun's motion multiplied by the difference between the Earth's diameter and the Sun's diameter, and then divided again by the daily motion in yojanas, result in the minutes of arc for the shadow (Rāhu) as it moves along the Moon's path.

Chapter Nine. The difference between the results arising from the slow and fast motions of the Sun and Moon should be applied as an addition or subtraction to the body (śarīra) according to whether the sign is Cancer or Leo and so forth, based on the union or separation of the signs. To this body, one should add or subtract the degrees of the peak of the product of its own [sine] values. Then, the minutes of arc of the orbs of depression (mauḍhya) of Mars and the others, multiplied by five and divided by the minutes of the orbs of depression at rising, are further multiplied by the shore (pulina) diminished by the Moon and increased by the lord of the place of rising; these are thus declared by some.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Itikaraṇapaddhati*. Now begins the ninth chapter: When the elapsed portion of the desired sign has reached its end, at an interval of one minute of arc (*prāṇakalā*) of the [sign's] motion (*cara*), one should perform the calculation; that is declared to be the ascendant (*lagna*) at the time of the end of the desired sign. (1)
The degrees of the interval between the desired time and the end-time of the previous day's ascendant, multiplied by ten, become the minutes of arc for the measure of the desired sign. (2)

The king of men is one who knows the shore, who is pleased by virtue, who is to be honored, who is worthy of choice, who is established, who is generous, and who is a lord of men; he is like turmeric, like the ocean, like a blow, like the water of the day, whose limbs are natural, who transcends, and who is unopposed. (3)

Vibhāva, tṛṇaudha, gajābha, dhaneśa, baleśa, dhṛtāśa, kalātmā, vipakṣa, kṣamokṣa, and nilānta—these, when preceded by vastra and increased in sequence, are the clear degrees (sphuṭāṃśāḥ) [of the planets]. || 4 ||

In the manual of ritual practice (*karaṇapaddhati*), the sage who is to be saluted is beloved; indeed, he who possesses a [pure] body is always worthy of worship. It is only fitting that the wise man is beloved in the world, and likewise, the son who is learned is cherished in his own station.

The Sun is in the ascendant; in the house of the native (the fifth) is the son, namely the planet Rāhu. Indeed, Mars is there, and the additive degrees from Aśvinī onwards are as follows in sequence: 6.

The task of the two *Dasras* (Aśvins) is assigned to Agni; Vāyu, Vasu, Ekapāt, Viśākha, and Śūrpa are the Saumyas (belonging to Soma). The others are the Yāmyas (belonging to Yama). These are the projections (*kṣepas*) of Varuṇa, Nairṛta, and Śūrpa, endowed with the divine [measure], the mountain, the serpent, and the digit (*kalā*).

The true longitudes of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) should be calculated as complete values, corrected for precession. Their true latitudinal components (krāntiguṇas) are likewise determined, corrected by their respective declinations (vikṣepas).

Having multiplied the sine of the obliquity by the maximum apsis-argument, and having multiplied the desired declination by that same argument, both [results] divided by the radius (trijyā) become suitable for addition or subtraction. (9)

The conjunction of these two when they are in the same direction, and their separation when in different directions, is the true declination for those situated on the circle of latitude, whose [sine] is the co-latitude of the true declination and whose amplitude is the oblique ascensional difference.

The multiplier, multiplied by the true declination and further corrected by the addition of the [ascensional] difference alone, is then multiplied by the maximum declination and divided by the maximum declination to yield the multiplier. (11)

The arc obtained by dividing the product of the [ascendant] sine and three signs by the sine of the true oblique ascension, added to three signs, shall be subtracted or added to the true oblique ascension added to three signs, depending on whether their directions are the same or different; this results in the midday ascension for that day. (12)

Then, having introduced the difference in one's own [ascensional] differences (*nijakalā*) into that [longitude], and having added three signs to it, one should—just as before—multiply the sine of its own amplitude (*svabhujāpamajyā*) by the obliquity (*kṣepa*) and divide by the cosine of the amplitude (*apamakoṭi*), in order to establish the *lagna* for the time of its own meridian transit. (Chapter Nine) 13.

Alternatively, having derived the various minute parts (*asukalā*) of the declination (*krānti*) from that [longitude] using the true [longitude] diminished by three signs (*tribhona*), one should add those minute parts to the true [longitude] when it is increased by three signs. Then, taking the product of the two declinations, dividing by the product of half the radius (*ardhavistṛti*) and the sine of latitude (*yujyā*), and finding the arc [of that result], one should apply it as positive or negative to the two declinations—depending on whether they are of different or the same sign—to obtain the time of midday. (14)

Hara (the divisor) shall be obtained by dividing the koti of the argument by its own koti multiplied by the sine of the argument, and then subtracting that from the maximum koti (90°). The results for the corrected koti and the sine of the argument are obtained by multiplying the [original] argument by the [corrected] koti and dividing by the divisor. (15)

The correction for the argument (bhujāphala) is positive or negative in the semi-diameter (vyāsārddha) according to whether the sum or difference of the latitude (vikṣepa) and the sine of the anomaly (dorjyā) is taken; the square root of the sum of the squares of that [correction] and the result of the cosine (koṭiphala) shall be the karṇa known as the āyana. || 16 ||

Having multiplied the square root of ten million by half the radius, the result is the precession of the equinoxes (āyana). This is to be added to the true [longitude] when the [mean longitude] is in Capricorn or Cancer; however, when it is in Aries and so forth, it shall be otherwise (subtracted). (17)

Furthermore, if one should calculate the interval between the breaths (prāṇakalā) at that time, then it would be the time of depression (natakāla). This time called "depression" (nata), when added to three signs (tribha), becomes the time of subtraction for the midday calculation. || 18 ||

In the *Karaṇapaddhati*: from the time-ascendant at midday among the lunar mansions, subtract the time-ascendant at the end of the sign nearest to it; the degrees of the remainder, divided by six, become the elapsed *ghaṭikās* of that sign. (19)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Karaṇapaddhati.

Now begins the tenth chapter. Since the true latitudes of the planets have been stated in various ways by the wise, they are now examined and determined through observations made with instruments for the sake of clarity. (1)

In the northern hemisphere, when the product of the sine of the latitude and the cosine of the colatitude is subtracted from the radius, the result is known as the *apamaguṇa* (the sine of the declination). Its cosine is the sine of the amplitude. From the product of the radius and the cosine of the amplitude, divided by the sine of the day-arc and reduced to its arc, one obtains the time at the eastern horizon. This is positive in the forenoon; in the afternoon, it is diminished by three signs, and that becomes the time remaining until sunset (*vāyukāla*).

Alternatively, having added the product of the palas of the [local] latitude and the northern declination of the Sun, and divided by the trijyā (radius), one should apply this correction to the gnomon. Then, from the product of the sine of the latitude and the cosine of the Sun's declination multiplied by three, and divided by the square root of the sum of their squares, one should add [the result] to the ascendant at the time [of observation]. When the arc is subtracted, the time is in the eastern hemisphere; this is the midday time, and again, this same time diminished by three signs is the time of the wind (the setting sun). [Chapter Ten]
In the circle of the ghaṭikās, that point where [the sun] has touched is the meridian circle; that region is the time of wind, and it is called the time of depression (natakāla). || 4 ||

For all [planets], the true shadow is indeed the great shadow; when the arm-light is subtracted from the ascensional difference (kālalagna), that shall then be the time of culmination (natakāla). || 5 ||

Having calculated that [latitude] by assuming the oblique ascensional difference (natakāla) as the arm (bhuja) directed toward the opposite direction, one should again [calculate] the square of the true declination using the true co-latitude (sphuṭāpakramakoṭi).
Having performed [the operation] with the maximum limit, the displacement (vikṣepa) is obtained by dividing that by three times the life-span; one should then bring that limit together.

Again, having multiplied the correction-factor by the true declination, the sine of the argument (doḥjyā) produced from the time of the wind (vāyukāla), increased by three signs, is divided by the koti of the latitude (vikṣepakoṭi). This result is multiplied by the final declination and divided by the maximum declination; it is then converted into an arc. Depending on whether the product of the signs is even or odd, the time of the wind (vāyukāla) becomes corrected. (Verse 8)

Alternatively, when the time of the sun’s meridian transit has been obtained, one should multiply the sine of the [local] latitude by the product of the [ascensional] difference and the maximum declination, and divide by the product of the hypotenuse and the co-latitude; the result [is the desired correction]. (9)

One should also apply one’s own debt (longitude correction) by adding or subtracting the sine of the obliquity of the ecliptic according to whether the sum or difference of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon is less than six signs. This is the tenth chapter in the *Karaṇapaddhati*. When this [sum or difference] is diminished by three signs, one should again apply the precession of the equinoxes (ayanāṃśa) in reverse; thus it shall be its own true value. || 10 ||

Those who study this entire calculation, endowed with sound reasoning, shall become the foremost among the people of mathematicians on earth. Moreover, by means of the specific movement [of the planets], they experience intensely the pure state of Viṣṇu, who is equal to time, and thus go to His abode. (11)

And thus, a certain sacrificer born in the village named Śivapura has composed this work called *Karaṇapaddhati*, which is of the nature of a Tantra; having thoroughly examined this [work] whose calculations are distressing, may the virtuous who understand what is stated here be filled with satisfaction. (12)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Karaṇapaddhati. May there be auspiciousness!
